newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks seen continuing correction.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks seen continuing correction.

text.p: The mood of correction that has hit the Tokyo market following a recent surge is expected to persist in the coming week, brokers said.

The extent and length of the correction would depend greatly on external factors, they added. Wall Street's performance as well as yen/dollar rates held the possibility of sending the Tokyo benchmark down sharply.

"Stocks have been rising recently on excessive buying by pension funds," said Noboru Yorita, Tachibana Securities general manager. "If something happens to stall the buying, the Nikkei average could soften to the 19,500 level."
The 225-share Nikkei average had risen about 10 percent in the new business year started April 1.
But it slipped 259.03 points or 1.29 percent to end at 19,802.78 on Friday, closing below the 20,000 threshold for the first time that week.
The yen's rise against the dollar to above the 123 yen level on Friday, the first time it had reached that level in about a month, brought on profit-taking of blue-chip export-oriented shares.
Pension funds as well as foreign investors were also sellers.
"The mood is cautious after the recent sudden rise and stocks need a break." Hideyuki Ohkoshi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities, said.

"But turnover has been increasing steadily, buying interest has been showing signs of expanding and foreign investors' purchases are still mostly limited to laggards -- all signs that the indices have more room to rise again."

But some brokers said the market was close to reaching a consensus that maintaining gains above 20,000 would be difficult, especially since there were no solid factors to drive the index higher and market fundamentals remained little changed.

But brokers said public and pension funds with their allocations for the new year were still good customers with much buying power. The downside was not likely to be very deep as long as they have the potential to buy.

"New money and investors switching from bonds to stocks is brightening sentiment, but investors will probably take profits while the going is good," a trader at a foreign brokerage said. "After that, attention will shift to earnings announcements and strategies will be cobbled accordingly."
Nomura Securities Co Ltd strategist Masaaki Higashida said that the only entities with the power to pick up where the pensions leave off were foreign investors.
"Everyone will look to foreigners with hope," he said. "But for them to buy, Japan must clean up the bad-loan problems in its financial sector," he added.
